Machu Picchu · Anatomy

How the Inca built Machu Picchu

Dry-laid granite on terraces that drain. Click a part, fit the block yourself, or make it rain.

Ashlar wall

Temple walls are coursed granite ashlar laid dry, with no mortar. The courses get lower towards the top, the face leans back a few degrees, and niches and doorways narrow upwards, all of which help the wall ride out earthquakes. It stands on a foundation course sunk into the terrace fill.

Fitting a block

Each block was fitted by trial and error, and the joint was cut into the stone below it. Lowered onto its seat, the block packed the stone dust hard where the two touched; then it was lifted off and those high spots on the seat were pounded down with hammerstones, again and again until the joint closed. Jean-Pierre Protzen tried it: one joint took him 90 minutes.

The pole on its log crib is a reconstruction: how the blocks were lifted is not recorded.

Try itDrag the pole down to lift the block, click the packed dust to pound it, and let go to read the gap.

Stone and tools

The granite came from a quarry on the ridge itself: blocks were picked from rockfalls or pried loose along the rock's natural cracks. They were shaped by pounding with hammerstones, river cobbles tougher than the granite, heavy ones for roughing and small ones for finishing, without iron tools. The bosses left on the faces were probably for ropes and levers to bear on.

Moving the stone

The Inca had no wheeled carts and no animals that could pull stone: a llama carries only about 30 kg. Big stones were moved by people, with ropes and levers. At Machu Picchu the stone was quarried on the spot, so the hauls were short.

At Ollantaytambo a construction ramp still runs from the quarries across the river up to the temple, with some 80 abandoned blocks along it, the “tired stones”. The architect Jean-Pierre Protzen found polish and scratches on some of them: they were dragged over the ground.

Garcilaso de la Vega tells that more than twenty thousand men dragged one huge stone for Sacsayhuamán on thick ropes, half pulling in front and half holding it back on the slopes.

Try itDrag the end of the rope to haul the spare stone; the readout shows how many people it takes.

Terrace wall

Terrace walls are rougher fieldstone, built leaning back into the slope so the fill pushes them into the hill rather than over. They hold the fill against the steep mountainside and make flat ground to farm and build on.

Try itMake it storm on a clay fill to see the wall bulge.

Drainage fill

Most of the work is underground. Behind the wall the terrace is built in layers: big rubble on the bedrock, then gravel, then sand, then topsoil. Rain soaks straight through to the rubble and drains away, so the fill never turns to mud.

Try itSwitch to a clay fill and a storm to see why it matters.

Drains and channels

Water that reaches the rubble leaves through drains in the terrace walls and runs away along stone channels. The city has more than a hundred drains, part of the reason it has survived five centuries of heavy rain.

Earthquakes

Machu Picchu sits on a web of geological faults, and the Andes shake often. The walls lean inwards, doorways and niches narrow at the top, and dry-laid ashlar is thought to let each block slip a little and settle back, so the walls ride out quakes that crack stiffer masonry.

In the 1950 Cusco earthquake many Inca walls stood while colonial buildings on top of them were damaged.

Try itShake the table to compare a dry wall with a mortared one.

in use from c.1420 · 2,430 m altitude · ~60% of the work underground · ~2 m of rain a year. Machu Picchu · Anatomy

Hauling stone up a ramp

How the Inca moved their largest stones, at Ollantaytambo and Sacsayhuamán: what the sources say, and what is still not known.

What the sources say

  1. The Inca had no oxen and no carts. Stones were dragged by the strength of men's arms on thick ropes, up and down steep slopes.

    Garcilaso de la Vega, 1609

  2. On a slope, half the people pulled the stone from in front and the other half held it back with ropes from behind, so it would not run away downhill.

    Garcilaso de la Vega, 1609

  3. For Sacsayhuamán, Pachacuti ordered 20,000 men brought in from the provinces. Work for the state was owed as mit'a: turns of labour that each community took in rotation.

    Pedro Cieza de León, 16th century

  4. At Ollantaytambo the ramp from the quarries climbs at 8° to 12° and is 4 to 8 m wide, cut into the hillside behind retaining walls. Where the ground allowed, blocks went down slides instead: one drops about 250 m at 40° to the river.

    Jean-Pierre Protzen, 1985

  5. Some 80 blocks lie abandoned along that ramp, the “tired stones”. Polish and scratches on some of them show they were dragged over the ground.

    Jean-Pierre Protzen, 1985 and 1993

  6. In a modern test, dozens of villagers from Ollantaytambo dragged a 10-tonne stone uphill on ropes for almost a mile.

    NOVA, 1994, as reported later

What is still not known

  • Whether blocks rode on wooden sledges or went straight over the ground. Sledges worked with levers are an architect's proposal (Vince Lee), not a find.
  • Whether rollers were used. The only report, of wooden rollers under a block, is second-hand and dates from 1946.
  • How many people moved each block. No count survives, and the chroniclers' figures are traditions. With this model, 20,000 people could drag several hundred tonnes up a 10° ramp, far more than any stone at these sites.
  • Whether the track was wetted or spread with clay to help the stone slide. No evidence has been found either way.
  • How the blocks were raised into the wall. Protzen suspected earth embankments; no record says.

Force uses friction of 0.5 and 0.3 kN per person. Cadence, speed, rope motion and lever work are illustrative; no historical rhythm or speed is recorded. The two lever workers are shown separately and add no force to the calculation. Machu Picchu’s stone was quarried locally, so its hauls were short.
